title: How a CT Fellowship Helped One Young Pastor Find His Creative Community
summary: In 2024, Elijah Ramzy stumbled across an ad for CT’s inaugural Young Storytellers Fellowship. The message alerted him that it was the last day before applications closed. Elijah, a pastor and writer from the Dallas area, loves all things creative. Whether short stories, devotionals, essays, or poetry, writing is his outlet for processing what he  Read more...   The post  How a CT Fellowship Helped One Young Pastor Find His Creative Community  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 2024年，以利亚·拉姆齐偶然看到一则广告，是关于《基督教今日报》（CT）首届青年故事撰稿人奖学金的。这条消息提醒他，今天是申请截止前的最后一天。以利亚是来自达拉斯地区的牧师兼作家，他热爱一切与创意有关的事物。无论是短篇小说、灵修文章、散文还是诗歌，写作都是他处理所思所想的渠道。阅读更多……这篇文章《CT奖学金如何帮助一位年轻牧师找到他的创意社群》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。

title: From 1956 to 1971 to Today
summary: “Between my husband and I, we have subscribed to Christianity Today since 1971,” Cheryl Stacey tells me. “I have been a longtime supporter of Christianity Today.” Cheryl Stacey and her late husband, Dennis, have subscribed to Christianity Today for 55 years. “[During] one of our moves, I found ten boxes of old Christianity Today journals  Read more...   The post  From 1956 to 1971 to Today  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: “我和丈夫从1971年起就订阅《今日基督教》。”谢丽尔·斯泰西（Cheryl Stacey）告诉我。“我一直是《今日基督教》的长期支持者。” 谢丽尔·斯泰西和她已故的丈夫丹尼斯订阅《今日基督教》已有55年。“[在]我们的一次搬家中，我发现了十箱旧的《今日基督教》杂志。阅读更多……这篇题为《从1956年到1971年再到今天》的文章最初发表在《今日基督教》上。
title_zh: 从1956年至1971年，直至今日

title: To Save the World, We Need Good Dads
summary: “Fathers are the most important men in any community, anywhere, ever.” This bold and perhaps controversial claim captures the essence of Anthony B. Bradley’s belief that the fate of children, the family, American society, and perhaps even the free world depends upon good fathers. After reading his new book, The Fatherhood Effect: Consequences of a  Read more...   The post  To Save the World, We Need Good Dads  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: “在任何社区、任何地方、任何时候，父亲都是最重要的男人。” 这一大胆且可能颇具争议的论断抓住了安东尼·B·布拉德利（Anthony B. Bradley）的信念核心，即子女、家庭、美国社会，甚至可能是整个自由世界的命运都取决于好父亲。在读完他的新书《父性效应：缺席父亲对孩子、家庭、社会和国家的影响》后， 阅读更多……   这篇文章《要拯救世界，我们需要好爸爸》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。
title_zh: 为了拯救世界，我们需要好爸爸

title: Contemplative Prayer Is for Protestants Too
summary: It was a typical Monday night. My toddler was shrieking in her highchair, my dog was barking so ferociously there must have been an assassin at the door, and I was in the kitchen just trying to keep dinner from burning. My senses were overloaded, and I was tired. I recalled Brother Lawrence, another Christian  Read more...   The post  Contemplative Prayer Is for Protestants Too  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 这是一个典型的周一晚上。我的幼儿在餐椅上尖叫，我的狗汪汪叫得凶狠无比，仿佛门外有刺客，而我则在厨房里努力防止晚餐烧焦。我的感官超负荷，我感到疲惫不堪。我想起了另一位基督徒劳伦斯弟兄。阅读更多……这篇文章《默想祈祷也适合新教徒》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。
title_zh: 沉思祈祷也适用于新教徒

title: I Do Not Understand Why I Scroll
summary: We know that we are addicted to our screens and we know that this is bad. It is unclear whether this knowledge is having much affect on our behavior. We continue to check our phones while waiting at the bus stop, sitting through a sermon, standing in the checkout line, or dissociating at a family  Read more...   The post  I Do Not Understand Why I Scroll  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 我们知道自己沉迷于屏幕，也知道这不好。目前尚不清楚这种认识是否会对我们的行为产生很大影响。我们在公交车站等车、听完一场布道、站在收银台排队或在家庭聚会上神游时，仍然会不停地查看手机。阅读更多……文章《我不明白我为什么会刷手机》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。
title_zh: 我不明白我为什么会刷屏

title: Will We See Our Pets in Heaven?
summary: Since the 2004 publication of my book titled Heaven, I’ve heard easily a thousand questions about Heaven and the New Earth. The questions I hear most often are these: Will there be animals in Heaven? and, more specifically, Will our pets be there?One person wrote, “We are mourning the loss of our cat. He was hit by a  Read more...   The post  Will We See Our Pets in Heaven?  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 自2004年我的《天堂》一书出版以来，我听到的关于天堂和新地的问题不下千个。我最常听到的问题是：天堂里会有动物吗？更具体地说，我们的宠物会在那里吗？有人写道：“我们正在为失去爱猫而哀悼。它被……撞了。阅读更多……这篇文章《我们会在天堂见到我们的宠物吗？》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。
title_zh: 我们会在天堂见到我们的宠物吗？

summary: Wesley “Wes” Huff, a Christian influencer whose videos defending the historical accuracy of the Bible have been viewed nearly 30 million times, apologized Thursday for plagiarizing his academic work. “I have plagiarized the work of others,” he said in a post on X. “This was wrong, and it was sinful. Over the years, I allowed  Read more...   The post  Wesley Huff Apologizes for Plagiarism  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 基督教网红韦斯利·“韦斯”·赫夫（Wesley “Wes” Huff）的视频捍卫圣经的历史准确性，这些视频的观看次数已接近3000万次。周四，他为剽窃自己的学术作品而道歉。他在X上发帖称：“我剽窃了别人的作品。这是错误的，也是有罪的。多年来，我允许……阅读更多……这篇文章《韦斯利·赫夫就剽窃行为道歉》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。

title: The People of God Are a People Who Feast
summary: With November comes the commencement of an all-too familiar American holiday tradition: the decadent food indulgences of our Thanksgiving and Christmas festivities followed by the anxious dieting of our New Year’s resolutions. I came of age at the height of the diet culture of the ’90s and early 2000s. I was never diagnosed with an  Read more...   The post  The People of God Are a People Who Feast  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 随着11月的到来，一个再熟悉不过的美国节日传统拉开了帷幕：在感恩节和圣诞节的庆祝活动中大快朵颐，随后又因新年决心而焦虑地节食。我成年时正值20世纪90年代和21世纪初的节食文化盛行期。我从未被诊断出患有……阅读更多……这篇文章《上帝的子民是喜宴的子民》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。
title_zh: 上帝的子民是喜宴的子民

title: Your Riches Are Stored Up in Leonida
summary: Millions of real people waited in a real line to visit a fake place. It’s called Leonida—a parody depiction of the state of Florida—and it’s home to swamps, strip malls, beaches, penthouses, and a fake population of people with an unusually high tolerance for public disorder. Leonida exists within Grand Theft Auto VI, a buzzy  Read more...   The post  Your Riches Are Stored Up in Leonida  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 数百万真人排着真队，等待参观一个虚构之地。它名叫利奥尼达，是对佛罗里达州的戏仿描绘，这里有沼泽、商业街、海滩、顶层公寓，还有一群对公共秩序混乱有着异常高容忍度的虚构居民。莱奥尼达存在于备受瞩目的《侠盗猎车手6》中。阅读更多……这篇文章《你的财富储存在莱奥尼达》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。

summary: Artist and author Sho Baraka recently traveled to East Palo Alto, California, to visit StreetCode Academy, a nonprofit that aims to provide low-income communities with the tech skills they need to make a living in Silicon Valley, or pursue entrepreneurship and innovation. In this short documentary from CT’s Big Tent Initiative, Baraka interviews StreetCode cofounder  Read more...   The post  The Kids, Aunties, and Uncles Building Websites  appeared first on  Christianity Today .
summary_zh: 艺术家兼作家肖·巴拉卡（Sho Baraka）近日前往加利福尼亚州东帕洛阿尔托，参观了StreetCode学院。这是一家非营利组织，旨在为低收入社区提供在硅谷谋生或从事创业和创新所需的技术技能。在这部来自《今日基督教》“大帐篷计划”的短纪录片中，巴拉卡采访了StreetCode的联合创始人。阅读更多……这篇文章《孩子们、阿姨们和叔叔们正在搭建网站》最初发表在《今日基督教》上。

title: Pope Francis' diary recounts spiritual crisis, visions of Satan and Hell: 'Eyes of fire'
summary: Newly published entries from the private diary of Pope Francis recount the late pontiff's spiritual torment, which reportedly included three supernatural encounters with Satan and a vision of Hell amid the Chilean sex abuse scandal in 2018.
summary_zh: 新近发布的教宗方济各私人日记条目记述了这位已故教宗的精神折磨，据报道，其中包括在2018年智利性侵丑闻期间与撒旦的三次超自然遭遇以及对地狱的幻象。
title_zh: 教宗方济各的日记讲述了精神危机、撒旦和地狱的幻象：“燃烧的眼睛”
author: Jon Brown

title: Ex-Disney animator says executives asked for homosexual animals entering Noah's Ark
summary: A former Disney animation artist who worked on “The Lion King” and other Disney classics has claimed that studio executives once asked him to include same-sex animal couples in his retelling of the biblical story of Noah's Ark.
summary_zh: 一位曾参与《狮子王》和其他迪士尼经典作品的迪士尼动画师声称，工作室高层曾要求他在重述圣经中诺亚方舟的故事时，加入同性动物伴侣。
title_zh: 前迪士尼动画师称，高管要求将同性恋动物纳入诺亚方舟
author: Ian M. Giatti

title: Calvin Robinson garners visa review after his comments about Jews spark backlash
summary: Federal government officials are reportedly reviewing the visa status of British clergyman Calvin Robinson after his recent comments suggesting that Jews should be driven out of the United States.
summary_zh: 据报道，联邦政府官员正在审查英国牧师卡尔文·罗宾逊的签证状态，此前他最近发表言论，建议将犹太人驱逐出美国。

title: Pastor, teacher gets 10 years prison for seeking sex with 15-year-old in FBI sting
summary: A Louisiana pastor and elementary school teacher has been sentenced to 10 years in federal prison for attempting to entice what he believed was a 15-year-old girl into sexual activity.
summary_zh: 一名路易斯安那州的牧师兼小学教师因企图引诱他以为是15岁女孩的未成年人进行性行为而被判处10年联邦监狱徒刑。

author: Ryan Foley

title: Lock of George Washington's hair sells for $4K at auction
summary: A piece of American history changed hands Saturday when a lock of George Washington’s hair sold for $4,000 at auction, according to South Carolina-based Richmond Auctions. The buyer’s identity is unknown.
summary_zh: 据南卡罗来纳州里士满拍卖行（Richmond Auctions）消息，周六，一缕乔治·华盛顿的头发在拍卖会上以4000美元的价格易手，一段美国历史就此易主。买家的身份尚不清楚。
title_zh: 乔治·华盛顿的一缕头发在拍卖会上以4000美元的价格售出
author: Samantha Kamman

title: Peter Hitchens says 'GTA 6' needs a church, 'under­mines 2,000 years of Chris­tian civil­iza­tion'
summary: British commentator Peter Hitchens has called "Grand Theft Auto VI" "electronic poison" that undermines Christian civilization after he failed to find a church for his character in Vice City.
summary_zh: 英国评论员彼得·希钦斯（Peter Hitchens）在未能为自己的角色在罪恶都市中找到教堂后，将《侠盗猎车手6》称为“电子毒药”，认为其破坏了基督教文明。
title_zh: 彼得·希钦斯表示，《GTA 6》需要一座教堂，否则将“破坏2000年的基督教文明”

title: Southern Baptist Theological Seminary cuts ties with Kanakuk over camp child abuse allegations
summary: Southern Baptist Theological Seminary has cut ties with the Kanakuk Institute over its links to Kanakuk Kamps, which is under fire for allegations of child abuse.
summary_zh: 南方浸信会神学院（Southern Baptist Theological Seminary）已与卡纳库克学院（Kanakuk Institute）断绝关系，原因是该学院与卡纳库克营地（Kanakuk Kamps）有联系，而后者正因涉嫌虐待儿童而备受指责。
title_zh: 南方浸信会神学院因坎纳库克营地虐童指控而与其断绝关系

summary_zh: 今年的活动包括“圣诞儿童行动”的首次尝试。撒玛利亚钱包已获得许可，可以将鞋盒礼物从美国带入委内瑞拉。
title_zh: “Operation Christmas Child”活动结束了为期一周的物资收集工作，目标是收集1280万件物资，并计划首次向委内瑞拉运送物资

title: Crosspoint Church petitions Supreme Court over Maine's LGBT rules for school tuition program

summary_zh: 在食品价格上涨之际，美国各地的教会为有需要的家庭提供了数千份感恩节餐食，其中一家教会动员了当地橄榄球队的成员，另一家教会则带领数十人归信基督。

title: The Church Needs to Know Its History
summary: Readers of this first volume of ‘Church History for Everyone’ won’t get a complete understanding of church history, but DeYoung provides a doorway through which ordinary Christians can learn to explore primary sources and more comprehensive surveys on their own.
summary_zh: 我脸书留言的档案里 藏着一个叫凯西的寡妇的遗言 她感谢我在每周的圣经研究中使用教会历史. 她喜欢了解早期教会的殉道者和朝圣者. 作为一位在教会史上攻读博士学位的资深牧师,这是我需要的保证。 我们的信息线以凯西描述她的化疗结束.
title_zh: 教会需要了解自己的历史
content: Deep in the archives of my Facebook messages sits a note from a widow named Kathy. She thanked me for using church history in our weekly Bible studies. She loved learning about the early-church martyrs and the pilgrims. As a newly minted senior pastor pursuing a PhD in church history, this was the reassurance I needed. Our message thread ended with Kathy describing her chemo treatments. Like Faithful in John Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (a story new to her that strengthened her fight with cancer), Kathy endured her trials and entered the Celestial City. I usually have to defend the benefits of history to other pastors and friends of mine—but rarely with church members. I mostly encounter excitement when I direct Christians to our family history. In Church History for Everyone: The Story of Christianity from the Fall of Jerusalem to the Dawn of the Reformation , Kevin DeYoung, pastor of Christ Covenant Church and associate professor of systematic theology at Reformed Theological Seminary (Charlotte), blends rich doctrine with a pastoral tone. It’s the first of two planned volumes. DeYoung writes, “I intend this book to be a popular history rather than professional history, which means I am writing to be understood by ordinary people who are eager to learn but are not experts” (3). He’s successful in that effort. I wish Kathy could have read this book; it’s a church history for the church. History for the Church How is church history for the church actually for the church ? Well, words on a page are costly. Just like a pastor needs to cut more of his preparation and study out of his sermons than he’d like, a church history book for everyday Christians needs to value the reader’s attention. This means accepting that not every believer has the bandwidth to process all the names and details from church history we might want him or her to. There’s so much to digest, and the practical value of these names, dates, and specialized terms often don’t stick in the minds of casual readers. It’s easy for the stay-at-home mom or busy mechanic to delve into a church history book and quickly lose steam. On the other hand, oversimplifying in an attempt to make a book more accessible can move an argument from truth and falsehood. The story of our past needs the proper names, dates, and details to lead readers to experience the fruit of good historical learning. DeYoung attempts a near-impossible task: to write an introduction to church history that’s true (factually sound), good (encourages the church), and beautiful (enjoyable to read). He checks those boxes. Biographical Emphasis The most compelling histories are told through people, not periods. That explains why, “instead of a chronological encyclopedia version of history,” DeYoung takes “a biographical approach” (6). We get stories about figures like Irenaeus, Perpetua and Felicity, Athanasius, and Jan Hus. We read of Hus, As a pastor, Hus was passionate and sometimes hotheaded. His sermons also displayed a witty sense of humor. . . . Compared to most men of his age, he was not poor, but neither did he amass any fortune or have family estates to retire to. Even later when his enemies charged him with many faults and crimes, they never charged him with the typical list of priestly sins: drunkenness, sexual immorality, laziness, or opulence. (351) This approach has downsides, of course. A lot of important information gets left out. However, DeYoung recognizes that “when the author tells a story, there is a better chance that the reader might keep reading” (8). The most compelling histories are told through people. The biographical approach reinforces the fact that history often isn’t just about information transfer. “The goal in telling church history has been—for most of church history—a deliberate attempt at inspiration,” DeYoung observes. For example, “[Athanasius] wanted Christians in the fourth century to reach the inescapable conclusion that Antony was a hero, and that what he believed and how he lived had immediate lessons for followers of Christ everywhere” (71–72). From the earliest centuries, Christians have told the stories of other Christians. Accounts of Polycarp’s martyrdom to Foxe’s Book of Martyrs have inspired faithfulness for centuries. In recent years, John Piper’s short biographies and Stephen Nichols’s 5 Minutes in Church History podcast have awakened new appreciation for deeper studies of the past among laypeople. When we study church history, our doctrines and interpretations don’t remain in the abstract but get attached to names, faces, and places. We learn to see how our lives participate in the grand story of God thwarting Satan’s attempts to overwhelm the church. Novel Contribution Though a number of solid introductions to church history already exist, this first volume of Church History for Everyone fills an important niche. Almost every seminarian who has taken a class on the history of Christianity is familiar with Justo L. González’s two-volume The Story of Christianity . These works have offered classrooms a standard introduction to church history for more than 40 years. However, I’ve never directed church members to these works because they clock in around 1,000 pages total and include a lot of details about people, places, and events, without much theological commentary. We learn to see how our lives participate in the grand story of God thwarting Satan’s attempts to overwhelm the church. Many of God’s people want more than facts and narrative. This is why I’ve recommended Bruce Shelley’s Church History in Plain Language or Nick Needham’s five-volume 2,000 Years of Christ’s Power . Shelley writes with great clarity. Needham masterfully weaves the flow of church history with insight and precision. But I still offer caveats when recommending these works to church members because, as plain as the writing may be, the content is dense and filled with the nuance, historical data, and name indexes that stretch multiple pages. A chasm yawns between the academy and the pews that leaves many Christians wondering whether they’re looking at a textbook when they see it’s got “church history” on the cover. DeYoung demonstrates remarkable discipline as a trained historian as he writes this book by leaving many footnotes, narrative rabbit trails, and theological debates out of the final product. But that’s what makes this book so useful. Readers of this first volume of Church History for Everyone won’t get a complete understanding of church history, but DeYoung provides a doorway through which ordinary Christians can learn to explore primary sources and more comprehensive surveys on their own. I only wish that Kathy could have read this book; it would have helped sustain her on the journey to the Celestial City.
content_zh:
我脸书留言的档案里 藏着一个叫凯西的寡妇的遗言 她感谢我在每周的圣经研究中使用教会历史. 她喜欢了解早期教会的殉道者和朝圣者. 作为一位在教会史上攻读博士学位的资深牧师,这是我需要的保证。 我们的信息线以凯西描述她的化疗结束.
就像忠实于约翰·本扬的朝圣者进步(她的新故事加强了她与癌症的斗争)一样,凯西忍受了她的考验并进入了"天城". 我通常不得不为其他牧师和朋友捍卫历史利益, 当我把基督徒引向家族历史时,我大多会遇到兴奋.
在《人人教会历史:从耶路撒冷沦陷到改革黎明的基督教故事》中,Kevin DeYoung是基督盟约教会的牧师和改革神学院(Charlotte)的系统神学副教授,他把丰富的学说同牧歌融合在一起。 这是计划两卷中的第一卷。
DeYoung写道:“我打算这本书是一部受欢迎的历史而非专业历史,这意味着我写作是为了让渴望学习但并非专家的普通人理解。” (3)。 他的努力是成功的。 我希望凯西能读到这本书, 教会的历史 如何是教会的历史 实际上是教会?
页面上的字很贵 就像牧师需要从布道中切除更多的准备和学习, 这意味着接受并非每个信徒都有带宽处理我们可能希望他或她处理的教会史上所有名字和细节.
这些名称、日期和专门术语的实际价值往往不会停留在临时读者的脑海里。 家庭妈妈或繁忙的技工很容易钻研教会历史书籍, 另一方面,为了让一本书更容易取用而过分简化,可以将一个争论从真理和谎言中转移.
我们过去的故事需要适当的名字,日期和细节,以便引导读者体验好的历史学习的果实. DeYoung试图完成一个近乎不可能的任务:写一个教会历史的入门,这个入门是真实的(实际上声音),好的(鼓励教会),和美丽的(阅读的乐趣). 他检查那些盒子。
传记重点 最有说服力的历史是通过人们而不是通过时间讲述的。 这解释了为什么“而不是历史的分时间百科全书版本”,DeYoung采取“一种传记方式”(6)。 我们得到有关伊雷纳厄斯、佩佩图亚和费利西蒂、阿塔纳修斯和扬·胡斯等人物的故事。 我们读到胡斯,作为一个牧师,胡斯是热情的,有时是热头.
他的布道也表现出了幽默的机智.  . 相较于他这个年龄的大多数男人,他并不贫穷,但他也没有积累任何财富,也没有家庭地产可以退休. 甚至在后来他的敌人指控他有许多过失和罪行时,他们从未指控他有典型的祭司罪:醉酒,性不道德,懒惰,或奢侈.
(351) 这种做法当然有缺点。 许多重要信息被忽略. 然而,DeYoung承认,“当作者讲述一个故事时,读者继续阅读的机会就更大了”(8)。 最有说服力的历史通过人来讲述。 历史往往不只是信息传递。
" 讲述教会历史的目标 -- -- 对大多数教会历史来说 -- -- 是有意的启发, " De Young指出。 例如,“(阿塔纳修斯)希望第四世纪的基督徒能够得出一个不可回避的结论,即安东尼是英雄,他相信什么,他如何生活,对各地的基督追随者都有直接的教训”(71-72)。
从最早的几个世纪开始,基督徒就讲述了其他基督徒的故事. 数个世纪以来, Polycarp对Foxe的"烈士之书"的殉道事件, 近些年来,约翰·皮珀(John Piper)的短篇传记和斯蒂芬·尼科尔斯(Stephen Nichols)的"教会历史播客的5分钟"("5分钟")唤醒了外行对过去更深入的研究的新赞赏.
我们研究教会历史时, 我们学习如何看待我们的生活,
小说贡献 虽然已经存在一些对教会历史的扎实的介绍,但是这首"人人教会史"的第一卷填补了一个重要的位置. 几乎每名修习基督教历史的修道士,
这些作品为教室提供了40多年以来教堂历史的标准入门. 但我从未引导教会成员关注这些作品,
我们学习如何看待我们的生活, 许多人想要的不只是事实和叙事。 因此我推荐布鲁斯·雪莱的教会史, 舍利写作甚明.
尼德汉以洞察力和精准度巧妙地编织了教会历史的流传. 但我在向教会成员推荐这些作品时仍会提出警告,因为尽管写作可能很简单,内容很密集,并充满了细微的,历史数据,以及伸展多页的名称索引.
学校与修道院之间的隔阂令许多基督徒疑惑, 德永在写这本书时表现了杰出的纪律作为训练有素的历史学家,他留下了许多脚注,叙事兔踪迹,以及最后出品的神学辩论.
但正是这个原因使得这本书如此有用。 但DeYoung提供一条门道, 普通基督徒可藉以学习探索主要来源, 我只希望凯西能读这本书;
本来可以帮助她渡过天上之城
author: Travis Hearne

title: Help! My Bible Reading Feels Dead.
summary: Every passage takes its place in a larger drama. At the center of that drama stands a Person.
summary_zh: 她每天早上都读她的"圣经"11年. 她的日记。 她通过她的通道祈祷. 她通过阅读计划、学习圣经和献身指南而工作。
title_zh: 救命！我的读经生活毫无生气。
content: She has read her Bible every morning for 11 years. She journals. She prays through her passage. She has worked through reading plans , study Bibles, and devotional guides. And yet, sitting across from me in my study, she describes her Scripture reading with one word: dead. “I know I’m supposed to feel something,” she says. “But most days it just feels like going through the motions.” I’ve heard this confession more times than I can count from disciplined, sincere believers who do everything right and feel almost nothing. The standard prescriptions haven’t helped: Read more consistently, slow down and observe carefully, and find the application for your day. They’ve tried it all. The dryness remains. In most cases, the problem is a fundamentally misdirected reading method. Method We Were Handed Many of us were taught (implicitly or explicitly) to approach Scripture as primarily a collection of moral lessons, personal promises, and behavioral directives. We come to a passage asking, What am I supposed to do? What does God promise me here? How does this apply to my situation today? Scripture does instruct, promise, and call us to obey. But when this becomes our only lens, when we treat the Bible as a self-improvement manual with divine authority behind it, we’ve misread what kind of book it is. Moralistic Bible reading produces either pride when you keep up with the commands or despair when you cannot. Neither is an encounter with the living God . Moralistic Bible reading produces either pride when you keep up with the commands or despair when you cannot. Puritan writers such as Walter Marshall warned against what they broadly termed a “legal spirit”: treating God’s Word as a taskmaster instead of hearing in it the voice of a Father who acted in history to save a people for himself. Marshall’s classic Gospel Mystery of Sanctification remains the fullest treatment of this danger, and his diagnosis matches the wider Puritan tradition: The remedy was never more effort. It was a clearer sight of Christ. Road to Emmaus Changes Everything On the afternoon of the first Easter, two disciples walked from Jerusalem to Emmaus with shattered hopes and a Scripture they thought they understood. Then a stranger joined them on the road. “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Jesus didn’t give them a new application strategy. He gave them a new reading of the same Scripture they already possessed. Moses, the Prophets, the Psalms—all of it spoke of him. The entire redemptive history of Israel was moving toward him, finding its meaning in him, and flowing from him. The result wasn’t intellectual satisfaction but a burning heart. “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” (v. 32). This “burning” is what theologians call the fruit of redemptive-historical reading. When you read Scripture as God’s unfolding story of redemption , traced through creation, fall, promise, covenant, fulfillment, and consummation, every passage takes its place in a larger drama. At the center of that drama stands a Person. You’re being introduced, again and again, to him. Read the Whole Story Consider what this lens opens up in familiar passages. Leviticus’s sacrificial system, which modern readers so often experience as tedious, becomes luminous when read as the redemptive-historical preparation for the once-for-all sacrifice of the Lamb of God. Every slaughtered animal announces the same truth: Something must die; sin requires atonement; a substitute must bear what the guilty cannot. You arrive at Calvary, and the whole system resolves into its intended meaning. Every passage takes its place in a larger drama. At the center of that drama stands a Person. The psalms of lament, those raw and disorienting cries of abandonment, take on new weight when you see that the Son of God himself prayed them from the cross. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 22:1) isn’t only David’s prayer and your prayer; it’s Christ’s prayer, offered as a model for every broken human being who has ever felt forsaken (Matt. 27:46). You’re praying with your great High Priest. All the Scriptures concern him. That gravity, once felt, pulls everything into focus. Three Questions Careful reading, observation, and application remain essential. What changes is the frame those practices work within. Before asking what you should do, consider these three questions of your passage: 1. Where is this passage in the story of redemption? Is this text in the period of promise, covenant, or fulfillment? What was God doing here in the history of salvation? 2. How does this passage point toward or flow from the work of Christ? Every text exists within a story that culminates in him. 3. What does this reveal about the God who gave his Son? Scripture’s deepest purpose is the knowledge of God , and his fullest disclosure is the crucified and risen Son. These questions give application its proper weight. When you see what God has done in Christ, obedience becomes response instead of performance. You’re not working to earn anything. You’re responding to everything already given. Your Heart Can Still Burn My church member didn’t have a discipline problem. She had more discipline than most. She had been reading a love letter as an instruction manual, and instruction manuals don’t make hearts burn. The remedy for devotional dryness is learning to read Scripture the way its Author intended, as a unified, Christ-centered story of redemption, alive in every part, burning toward a consummation that has already broken into history on Easter morning. The stranger on the road to Emmaus is still opening the Scriptures. The question is whether we read them in a way that positions us to recognize him when he does.

“但大多数时候, 我听到这些忏悔的次数比我能数的多, 标准处方没有帮助:更一致地阅读、减速和仔细观察, 他们都试过了。 干燥犹存.
在大多数情况下,问题是一个根本错误的读取方法. 我们许多人(隐含或明确)被教导把《圣经》视为主要道德教训、个人承诺和行为指示的集合。 我们来到一个段落 问,我该怎么办? 上帝答应我什么? 这对我今天的处境有何影响?
圣经的确教导我们,答应我们,召唤我们服从。 但当这成为我们唯一的镜像时, 当我们把《圣经》当作一本有神圣权威的自我改进手册, 道德主义 圣经的读取,要么在遵守命令时产生自豪感,要么在不能时产生绝望感. 也没有遇到活着的上帝。
道德主义 圣经的读取,要么在遵守命令时产生自豪感,要么在不能时产生绝望感. 像沃尔特·马歇尔这样的清教徒作家警告说,他们通常称之为“法律精神 ” : 将上帝的话当作一个任务主管,而不是在其中听到一位历史上为拯救人民而行动的父亲的声音。
马歇尔经典的"福音圣洁之谜"(Ghosts Mystery of Sanctification)仍然是最充分地处理这种危险,他的诊断符合更广泛的"清教徒"传统: 补救办法从未如此努力。 更清楚地看到基督。
通往艾玛乌斯的路会改变一切 在第一次复活节的下午,两个门徒从耶路撒冷走去艾玛乌斯,带着破碎的希望和他们认为能理解的圣经. 然后一个陌生人在路上加入了他们 他从穆萨和众先知开始,在一切天经中,他都要对他们宣读他的故事。
耶稣没有给他们新的应用策略。 他使他们重新诵读他们已掌握的经典。 穆萨、众先知、众菩萨,都曾提及他。 以色列的整个红发历史都朝他走去,从他那里找到它的意义。 其结果不是智力满意,
“当他在路上和我们说话的时候,难道我们的心没有烧着吗?” 这种"燃烧"是神学家所说的"红色先发制人-历史读取"的果实. 当你把圣经读作上帝的救赎故事, 通过创造、倒下、承诺、契约、实现和完成, 每一段都在更大的戏剧中取而代之。
剧情的中心是人物 你不断被介绍给他。 阅读"全史" 考虑一下这个镜头在熟悉的段落中打开什么. 利维提库斯的"牺牲"制度,现代读者经常像乏味地体验,在读作红色的先发制人-历史的准备,一劳永逸地为"上帝的羔羊"作牺牲时会变得发光.
每个被屠宰的动物都宣布同样的真理:一定有东西会死;罪恶需要赎罪;替代者必须承担罪人所不能承担的. 你到达卡尔瓦里,整个系统 解决它的意图。 每个段落都以更大的戏剧取而代之. 剧情的中心是人物
哀叹的诗歌 那些生动和不听话的被抛弃的叫声 当你看到上帝之子自己从十字架上祈祷时 开始重来 “我的上帝,我的上帝,为什么你抛弃我?”(P. 22:1)不仅仅是大卫的祷告和你的祷告;而是基督的祷告,它作为每一个曾经感到被抛弃的破碎人类的典范(Matt. 27:46)。
你正在与你的伟大的大祭司祈祷。 所有经典都和他有关 这种引力,一旦感觉到,就把一切引向焦点. 三个问题仍然至关重要。 改变之处在于这些做法在框架之内起作用。 在问起你应该做什么之前,考虑一下你通过的三个问题: 1.赎罪故事中的这段话在哪里?
这是在承诺、盟约或实现的时期吗? 救赎史上上帝在这里做什么? 2. 这一段落如何指向或来自基督的工作? 每一个文字都存在于一个故事中,而这个故事最终会发生在他身上. 3. 这揭示了给儿子的神是什么?
圣经最深的旨意是了解上帝,他最充分地揭示了被钉在十字架上并升起的儿子。 这些问题给予适当重视。 当你看到上帝在基督中做了什么,服从就变成了回应而不是表现. 你没有工作来赚钱。 你正在回应已经给出的一切。
你的心仍然可以燃烧 我的教会成员没有纪律问题。 她的纪律比大多数人都强 她读过一封情书,
对奉献性干燥的补救是学习如何阅读《圣经》, 其作者打算用一个统一的、以基督为中心的故事来讲述赎罪, 在每一个方面都是活生生的, 在复活节的早晨,它已经进入历史。 前往艾玛乌斯路上的陌生人仍然在开"圣经".
问题是,我们是否在阅读这些内容时,能够使我们在认识他时认出他。

title: 5 Reasons Why It’s Hard to Discuss Our AI Fears
summary: Christians aren’t remotely ready for the age of AI. Learn more about it and be ready to draw the line.
summary_zh: Jensen Huang在Nvidia的出走(和在Nvidia的复职)的报导、大型科技公司的连锁失败以及关键基础设施的明显漏洞, 最近的对话使我得出了一个令人不舒服的结论:大多数基督徒还没有为AI时代做好远程准备. 这里有五个复杂因素 很难谈论AI。 1. 大赦国际不是单一的;
title_zh: 难以讨论我们对人工智能的恐惧的5个原因
content: Between the coverage of Jensen Huang’s departure from (and reinstatement at) Nvidia , the cascading failures in large tech companies , and the obvious cracks in critical infrastructure , many people are feeling acute uncertainty about technology . Recent conversations have led me to an uncomfortable conclusion: Most Christians aren’t remotely ready for the era of AI. Here are five complexities that make talking about AI difficult. 1. AI is not monolithic; it is a series of overlapping epochs. The first epoch of AI is the LLM stage (2022–present). This epoch began with the release of ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other models. The second epoch is the agentic AI stage that began this year. The epoch marks the introduction of AI bots such as OpenClaw, Grok Bot, and Muse. The third epoch, which hasn’t arrived yet but will likely begin in 2027 or 2028, is the physical AI stage. The beginning of this epoch will be marked by the arrival of robots (think Tesla’s Optimus robot) that use AI to replicate human actions in the wider world. As I have written elsewhere , these epochs will move and change at speeds faster than we can understand. 2. A wise posture toward AI looks different for four groups of Christians. These four groups (more could be added) are parents, pastors and ministry leaders, educators, and marketplace leaders. Each of these groups needs better education on AI. And after they have been educated, some groups may need to use AI more, and some need to use it less. Parents need to learn from the social media era and better protect their kids. We’ve seen how Gen Z was wrecked by social media apps. We can prevent a similar level of harm to Gen Alpha by making sure they’re not overexposed to AI while they’re young. Pastors and ministry leaders need to learn to develop greater discernment toward AI besides “I love it” or “I hate it.” The “I hate it” group needs to recognize legitimate uses for AI, especially in administrative, systematic, and process situations. The “I love it” group needs to know the serious dangers around cognitive off-loading, intellectual and spiritual malformation when using AI for sermon prep, and legal issues surrounding data. Educators, teachers, and administrators—especially those in Christian education contexts—need to better understand the technology and its neurobiological implications on young people. AI skills aren’t hard to acquire. Learning about harnesses, prompt engineering, MCPs, and markdown files on YouTube can take you from zero to 100 in a matter of hours. These tools don’t need to be incorporated in every grade or every subject. The biggest needs in Christian education should be spiritual formation, the cultivation of virtue, the discipline of reading books and long-form media, and the ability to craft analogy arguments that can be defended orally and in writing. For marketplace leaders, they need to know it’s reasonable to use AI for certain things and then not want it anywhere near other parts of your day. That is, admittedly, a difficult tension to hold. Many of us are in more than one of these four groups. It will take a great amount of wisdom to parse how to walk in wisdom with AI at our company and under the roof of our home. We need to learn how to appreciate the tech and how we can use it in one domain while insisting it not seep into another domain. It’s OK to want AI to make breakthroughs in medicine and to not want it break the intellectual supply chain of your pastor’s sermon prep. 3. We’re undereducated and overconfident about the tool we’re using all the time. The average person’s education levels about AI are uncomfortably low. This means low understanding on how this technology works, what it’s good at, what it struggles with, what we should use it for, what we shouldn’t use it for, and how to best use it. It’s OK to want AI to make breakthroughs in medicine and to not want it break the intellectual supply chain of your pastor’s sermon prep. At the same time, many people believe they know what they’re doing when they use AI. They put a prompt in and get a lengthy response back, so they assume they’re doing something right. But that is a naive approach. In reality, many Christians are on the Dunning-Kruger curve at the peak of “Mount Stupid” where they think they have a solid grasp of AI and yet they know next to nothing. I have recently been at a few different universities interacting with students, campus ministers, faculty, and administration. It has been illuminating. Departments fall all over the place terms of how they are thinking about AI. Departments who hate it probably need more understanding, and the folks who love it probably need more discernment. Anecdotally, I find the undereducation/overconfidence paradox at work among the students I’ve interacted with. When I polled several hundred students across multiple universities and departments, 80 percent of the students said they use AI daily. But when I followed up and asked them whether they knew what an AI harness was, what a markdown file was, or if they had heard the term “prompt engineering,” only one hand went up. Despite their lack of knowledge about AI, the students tend to show a lot more concern about AI than their professors do. Conversations I’ve had with faculty and administration weren’t much better; in many conversations, I found their ignorance of and confidence in AI more deeply concerning than their students’. I’ve heard administrators commend the use of AI for free cognitive behavioral therapy and for things even cringier than that. These are serious Christians with advanced degrees! It’s a huge problem. That’s why The Gospel Coalition has published a benchmark to show you what AI models do well regarding religious questions and where you should run in the other direction. 4. AI will forever change how humans acquire knowledge. As far back as humans remember, knowledge has transferred from one human mind to another through either embodied teaching or text. AI destroys that direct human-mind to human-mind chain and inserts itself as a middleman. This makes AI a kind of high priest of knowledge and creates an “ intellectual Strait of Hormuz .” 5. Everyone needs proactive rules about what they will and will not use AI for. Almost nobody that I interact with has developed proactive rules for when he or she does and doesn’t use AI. This is a big problem. Every new use case must have intellectual and spiritual justification before we adopt it. One such example for me is that I never use AI for wisdom. Knowledge, sometimes . Wisdom, never . Wisdom is for prayer, the Bible, books, and trusted advice from people. Drawing a line and sticking to it is essential. Way Forward On the one hand, I’m not surprised that Christians are behind the curve on AI. As the writers laid out in TGC’s new book The AI Apocalypse , this technology has both incredible opportunities and tremendous dangers. The news cycle related to Nvidia alone this week is impossibly fast to keep up with. To address this education gap I’m working with TGC’s women’s team to host a four-week, online interactive cohort on biblical wisdom for AI, starting in January. Every new use case must have intellectual and spiritual justification before adoption. On the other hand, I’m witnessing both uncritical adoption and unhelpful rejection among many Christians. If I were to prescribe a better way forward, I suggest three things. 1. Christians need to understand that AI isn’t one thing. In some use cases, AI extends common grace. In other use cases, AI is truly horrible. We should have the discernment to see both. 2. Christians should better educate themselves on how AI technology works, what it’s good at, where it struggles, and what we should and shouldn’t use it for. 3. Christians should draft clear, proactive rules rooted in a Christian worldview on when they will and won’t use AI and why.
content_zh:
Jensen Huang在Nvidia的出走(和在Nvidia的复职)的报导、大型科技公司的连锁失败以及关键基础设施的明显漏洞, 最近的对话使我得出了一个令人不舒服的结论:大多数基督徒还没有为AI时代做好远程准备.
这里有五个复杂因素 很难谈论AI。 1. 大赦国际不是单一的;它是一系列重叠的时代。 AI的第一个时代是LLM阶段(2022年-现在). 这个时代开始于ChatGPT,克洛德,双子座等模型的发行. 第二个时代是今年开始的代理AI阶段.
这个时代标志着AI bots的引入,如OpenClaw,Grok Bot,和Muse等. 第三个时代是体能AI阶段, 这个时代的开始将标志着机器人(Tesla's Optimus robot)的到来,他们利用AI在更广阔的世界中复制人类行动.
正如我在别处所写的那样 这些时代会以我们无法理解的速度移动和改变 2. 四个基督徒群体对大赦国际的明智姿态不同。 这四个团体(还可以增加)是父母、牧师和部委领导人、教育工作者和市场领导人。 每一个群体都需要更好的AI教育.
而在他们受过教育后,有些群体可能需要多使用AI,有些则需要少使用. 父母需要从社交媒体时代学习,更好地保护孩子. Gen Z如何被社交媒体的应用所破坏。 我们可以防止类似程度的伤害,
除了“我爱它”或“我恨它 ” , 牧师和部委领导人需要学会对AI产生更大的认知。 “我讨厌它”群体需要承认对大赦国际的合法用途,特别是在行政、系统和流程方面。
“我爱它”团体在使用AI进行布道准备时,需要了解认知卸载、智力和精神畸形以及围绕数据的法律问题方面的严重危险。 教育工作者、教师和行政人员,特别是基督教教育背景的人员,需要更好地理解技术及其对年轻人的神经生物影响。
AI技能并不难获得。 在YouTube上学习使用带,即时工程,MCP,和markdown文件,可以在数小时内将您从0带到100. 这些工具不需要纳入每个年级或每个科目。
基督教教育的最大需要应该是精神的形成,美德的培养,阅读书籍和长式媒体的纪律,以及能够编造可以口头和书面辩护的类比论点的能力. 对于市场领袖来说, 他们需要知道使用人工智能处理某些事情是合理的,
诚然,这是难以维持的紧张局势。 我们许多人属于这四组人中不止一组人。 要在我们的公司和我们家的屋檐下 和AI一起用智慧去解释 我们需要学习如何欣赏技术,以及如何在一个领域使用技术,同时坚持不要把它渗入另一个领域。
希望AI在医学领域取得突破, 3. 我们的教育不足,对我们一直使用的工具过于自信。 有关人工智能的平均教育水平低得令人不快。
这意味着人们对这种技术如何运作、它擅长什么、它与什么斗争、我们应该如何使用它、我们不应该使用它、以及如何最好地使用它缺乏了解。 希望AI在医学领域取得突破,
许多人相信, 所以他们认为自己做得对。 但这是一种天真的做法。 事实上,许多基督徒在“愚蠢山峰”上登上邓宁-克鲁格曲线,他们认为自己牢牢掌握了人工智能,却一无所知。
最近我在几所不同的大学与学生、校园部长、教职员工和行政人员互动。 它一直在发光。 各部门纷纷陷入对AI的看法。 讨厌它的部门可能需要更多的理解,喜欢它的人可能需要更多的分辨.
与我互动的学生工作时, 当我在多个大学和部门调查几百名学生时,80%的学生说他们每天使用AI。
但当我跟踪并问他们是否知道AI的用具是什么,什么是平分档案,或者他们是否听说过“即时工程”一词,只举出一只手。 尽管学生们对AI缺乏了解,但是他们往往比他们的教授对AI表现出更多的关注. 我与教职员工和行政人员的对话并不更好。
在很多对话中,我发现他们对大赦国际的无知和信任比他们的学生更深刻。 我听到管理者赞扬使用AI免费认知行为疗法, 他们是有高级学位的基督徒! 这是一个巨大的问题。
因此,福音联盟公布了一个基准,以显示AI模式在宗教问题上做得好,以及你应该往另一个方向跑。 4. 大赦国际将永远改变人类如何获得知识。 早在人类记忆中,知识就已经通过隐含的教义或文字从一个人类的思想转移到另一个人的思想.
AI摧毁了将人心直接指向人心的链条并插入自己作为中间人. 这让大赦国际成为知识的大祭司,并建立了一个“知识的霍尔木兹海峡”。 每个人都需要关于他们愿意和不会使用AI的主动规则. 与我交往的几乎没有人会制定主动的规则, 这是一个大问题。
每一个新的使用案例都必须有理智和精神上的理由,然后我们才能通过. 对我来说,一个例子是,我从来没有用AI来表达智慧。 有时候是知识 智慧,永远不要。 智慧是用于祈祷,圣经,书籍,以及人们信任的建议. 划出一条线并坚持下去至关重要。 前进之路 我并不感到惊讶,
正如TGC新书《启示录》所描述的, 本周仅与Nvidia有关的新闻周期无法跟上。 为了弥补这一教育差距,我正在与TGC的妇女团队合作,为AI主办为期四周的在线互动小组,介绍圣经智慧,从一月份开始。
每一个新的使用案例在通过前都必须有智力和精神上的理由. 我亲眼目睹许多基督教徒不批判性领养, 如果我要规定更好的前进道路,我建议做三件事。 基督徒需要明白, 在某些情况下,大赦国际给予共同恩惠。
在其他使用情况下,AI的确可怕. 我们应该有辨别力 来看到两者。 2. 基督徒应该更好地教育自己AI技术如何运作,它擅长什么,它在哪里挣扎,以及我们应该和不应该使用它。 基督徒应该起草明确、主动的规则, 植根于基督教的世界观,

title: Leverage Church History for Ministry
summary: Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss how pastors can use church history to strengthen their preaching, encourage their congregations, understand historic Christian beliefs, and learn from believers who have gone before us.

content: Why should pastors care about church history, and how can they use it in everyday ministry? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss why church history is more than a subject for scholars. They share practical ways pastors can draw from Christian biographies, historical events, and the early church to strengthen their preaching and help their congregations grow in faith. title: How to Preach to Workers
summary: The New Testament offers two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching.
summary_zh: 我还记得我第一次听到关于上帝设计工作的布道。 科林·史密斯牧师参加了一系列通过"十诫"的工作,他来到了安息日的第四个指挥. 我期待听到关于休息的有挑战性的话。 所以我很惊讶,当他用 他的布道的前半部分 谈论工作。
title_zh: 如何向工人传福音
content: I still remember the first time I heard a sermon on God’s design for work. Pastor Colin Smith was in a series working through the Ten Commandments, and he’d come to the fourth command about the Sabbath. I was expecting to hear challenging words about rest. So I was surprised when he spent the first half of his sermon talking about work. Because he’s a good exegetical preacher, Smith reminded us to pay attention to the part of the passage we might overlook: “Six days you shall labor, and do all your work . . .” (Ex. 20:9). For 16 minutes, Smith preached about God’s design for work. He explained how God modeled work in creation, crafting and making our world like a builder, engineer, and artist. And since humans were created in the likeness of this God, our labors are a significant part of what it means to represent him in the world. Then he started naming regular kinds of work—such as the school crossing guard who creates a zone of safety and protection for children. He shared example after example, even naming those who are were unemployed and looking for work as engaging in a form of dignified labor. They can please God as they trust him to provide and remain diligent to seek out what’s next. At the time, I was working a summer landscaping job between semesters at seminary. I took the job because it was necessary, not because I found it personally fulfilling or spiritually significant. I’d been subconsciously wanting to be done with mowing lawns and picking weeds so I could get back to the important work of studying Scripture. But God used Smith’s sermon to reorient my ordinary labor. Preaching with workers in mind is vital to shepherding a congregation. It reminds church members that work is a primary context for discipleship and helps them work out the implications of God’s Word where they spend a large portion of their time. The New Testament gives two paradigms for how preachers can consider workers in their teaching. Work as an Illustration of the Kingdom As the eternal, perfect Son of God, Jesus isn’t only Savior and Lord but also the most brilliant teacher the world has ever heard. Therefore, as preachers, we take his pedagogy seriously even as we learn his precepts and mimic his practices. Jesus often proclaims the good news by igniting people’s imaginations and explaining eternal truths in concrete realities, including the body (Matt. 6:22; 7:3–5; 24:7–8), nature (Matt. 6:28–29; Mark 11:23; Luke 17:6), and food (Matt. 13:33; John 6:35, 53–56). But Jesus’s most consistent metaphor for the truths of the kingdom is work and workers. Klaus Issler’s survey reveals that of the 37 parables in the Synoptic Gospels, 32 reference work or workers, representing 22 different work roles. In 25 of the parables, work is a main part of the storyline. Here are examples: The farmer sows the seed (Matt. 13). The faithful manager gives the servants of the household food at the proper time (Luke 12:42). Even an unjust judge will give a persistent widow justice (18:1–8). The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). A king going into battle should take counsel to see if he’s strong enough before he a ttacks (Luke 14:31). When Jesus describes what it meant to follow him and live in his kingdom, why does he use the ordinary language of work and workers? First, God’s self-disclosure is often wrapped in the language of work. For instance, he’s portrayed as a composer and performer (Deut. 31:19), a tentmaker (Job 9:8), a garment maker and dresser (29:14), a shepherd (Ps. 23:1–4), a builder (Prov. 8:27–31), a metalworker (Isa. 1:24–26), a potter (31:9), and a farmer (Hos. 10:11). If God is the original worker, it makes sense that the whole realm of work can teach us his ways. If God is the original worker, it makes sense that the whole realm of work can teach us his ways. Second, Jesus likely spent nearly six times as many years as a regular worker than he did in his public ministry—probably as a stonemason, either running a small family business or working as a day laborer. Wouldn’t it make sense that 17 or 18 years of regular work would inform the language of his teaching? It isn’t a coincidence that Jesus summarizes the implications of his teaching with the image of two builders: one who built on a sturdy foundation and one who built on sand (Matt. 7:24–27). Jesus knows by experience the ramifications of choosing the wrong foundation. So that’s the mental model he gives us to understand ways we can respond to his teaching. From Jesus to the Pulpit Jesus isn’t alone in using work as an illustration of the kingdom. Paul calls himself an expert builder who lays a foundation others build on (1 Cor. 3:10). He also instructs Timothy to meditate on the work of soldiers, athletes, and farmers to learn what it means to be a faithful pastor in Ephesus (2 Tim. 2:3–7). James too, in his final climactic call to wait for the Lord’s return, tells us to consider farmers who patiently wait for autumn and spring rains (James 5:7–8). When the New Testament writers explain what it means to walk with God, they regularly use examples from ordinary work. What might this mean for preachers today? As we explain the principles of God’s kingdom, how could we illustrate gospel truths with the work of baristas, software developers, accountants, realtors, or construction workers? How are God’s ways like a home inspector or a pilot? How is following him like the work of a middle manager or a plumber? To teach like Jesus and the writers of the epistles is to search out and proclaim the truth of the kingdom in the language of regular work. Along with making our teaching vivid, this dignifies people—in a unique way, their daily work is a picture of how God is at work in the world, and we can better understand who he is and what he calls us to if we look closely at the labor of his image-bearers. Work as an Application of the Gospel While Jesus primarily uses work to illustrate the kingdom, other New Testament writers mention work as a direct application of embracing the gospel. And even though the epistles aren’t sermons, they demonstrate how the apostles applied the gospel to common pastoral and contextual issues. For instance, Paul encourages the Corinthians, who have just been told of the wonders of the resurrection body, to know that their labor in the Lord isn’t in vain (1 Cor. 15:58). In a culture of persistent stealing, the Ephesians are called to do work that produces something good, so they’ll be able to give to those in need (Eph. 4:28). Bondservants with little power or agency are told to work diligently (6:5–9), knowing they’ll receive an inheritance as their reward and that their true Master is God himself (Col. 3:23–24). Those in Thessalonica who deem it more spiritual to constantly await God’s return without worrying about ordinary work are commanded to lead quiet lives, working with their hands (1 Thess. 4:11–12). James confronts boastful business leaders, saying they need to have a more God-dependent outlook (James 4:13–16) and that rich landowners who aren’t paying their workers can expect judgment (5:1–6). And Paul calls Philemon to envision a new working relationship with Onesimus, based not on power or status but on brotherly love and affection (Philem. 1:10–16). After articulating the gospel, the epistle writers consistently model that its application must be made clearly and contextually to people’s work. This suggests work should be a top-tier pastoral concern, with implications for the church’s regular teaching ministry. Work should be a top-tier pastoral concern, with implications for the church’s regular teaching ministry. Preaching to workers is a lifelong endeavor. Modeled by Jesus, the New Testament authors, and countless preachers throughout church history, in many times and in many places, the practice is rooted in pastoral curiosity and a desire to shepherd the people of God in their ordinary lives. 由于他是一个优秀的传教士,史密斯提醒我们注意我们可能忽略的那段话:"六天你必须努力,并做你所有的工作."(前20:9). 16分钟后,史密斯宣扬了"上帝"的工作设计. 他解释了上帝如何塑造我们的世界 像一个建筑师、工程师和艺术家

耶稣经常通过点燃人们的想象力和在具体现实中解释永恒的真理来宣布好消息,包括身体(Matt. 6:22;7:3–5;24:7–8),自然(Matt. 6:28–29;Mark 11:23;Luke 17:6)和食物(Matt. 13:33;John 6:35,53–56). 但耶稣对王国真理最一致的比喻是工作和工人.

像耶稣和史诗作家一样教书,就是用正作的语言去探寻并宣告王国的真理. 除了让我们的教学生动地进行外,这还使人们深受尊重——以独特的方式,他们的日常工作是描绘出上帝如何在世界上工作,如果我们仔细观察他的形象持有者的工作,我们就能更好地了解他是谁,以及他叫我们做什么。

title: The Gospel Coalition 2026 Book Awards
summary: The Gospel Coalition selects the best Christian books published in 2026 in our annual TGC Book Awards.
summary_zh: 保罗恳求蒂莫西将他的斗篷和书籍带给他,这有力地提醒人们在整个基督教历史(2 Tim. 4: 13)中书的重要性. 虽然死亡似乎接近,但保罗仍然渴望学习. 好书能加强灵魂.
title_zh: 2026 年福音联盟图书奖
content: Paul’s plea to Timothy to bring him his cloak and his books is a powerful reminder of how important books have been throughout Christian history (2 Tim. 4:13). Though death seemed near, Paul still longed to study. Good books can strengthen the soul. Amid the flood of new works published every year, it can be hard to find the sorts of books you would want with you on death row. The Gospel Coalition’s editorial team works hard to identify the best evangelical books published each year. This announcement is the culmination of months of hard work by a big team of book lovers. We receive nominations from publishers in 11 categories. Then our editors work together to recommend finalists in each category. Finally, a panel of judges reads each one carefully before casting their votes. The books are evaluated for the way they offer gospel-centered argument and application; include faithful and foundational use of Scripture, both Old Testament and New Testament; foster spiritual discernment of contemporary trials and trends; and encourage efforts to unite and renew the church. The result is a list of 22 books we recommend as helpful resources for the church and for individual believers. We hope you enjoy and are edified by them. You can find the books in a curated list at a discount in TGC’s online bookstore . Additionally, at the bottom of this article, you’ll find books that TGC has published this year, which were ineligible for our book awards. Congratulations to the winners of the 2026 TGC Book Awards. Andrew Spencer Books Editor Popular Theology Dane Ortlund, Finally Home: The Christian Hope of Heaven (Crossway) This world is beautiful, but it’s broken. Its sorrows remind us that something is terribly wrong; its joys whisper that something unimaginably better is coming. In Finally Home , Dane Ortlund turns our gaze toward that glorious future. With theological depth and the tenderness of a pastor who knows how to speak to weary souls, he brings the hope of heaven down to earth, speaking directly to the sorrows and struggles of everyday life. Here’s a book for Christians who need reminding that suffering will not have the last word, that Jesus will make all things new, and that the best is gloriously yet to come. You’ll finish these pages longing for home—and loving the Savior who will welcome you there. Award of Distinction Brett McCracken, The Wisdom of Sleep: How Rest Reveals God’s Truth and Revives Weary Souls (Zondervan) What if one of the most spiritual things you could do tonight is close your eyes and go to sleep? In The Wisdom of Sleep , Brett McCracken takes an activity we spend roughly a third of our lives doing and reveals its surprising theological significance. Pushing back against our culture’s relentless obsession with productivity, he draws on Scripture, science, and cultural insight to show that sleep isn’t a necessary evil or a strategy for getting more done. It’s a gift from God; a nightly reminder that we’re creatures, not the Creator; and a signpost pointing toward our eternal rest in Christ. Refreshingly practical and richly biblical, this book will leave you more grateful for the gift of sleep and more amazed by the God who never slumbers. Judges: Joshua Chatman, Juan Sánchez, Matt Smethurst, Laura Spaulding Ministry Tony Payne , Let the Word Dwell Richly: The Vital Power of the One-Another Word (Matthias Media) Evangelicals remain steadfastly committed to the ministry of God’s Word. And in our Reformed tradition, the sermon—public proclamation of the Word—rightfully takes center stage in our worship. Yet in our emphasis on expositional preaching, have we overlooked the Word ministry God gives to every Christian? Have we neglected the one-another word the New Testament writers repeatedly commend? Those are the questions Tony Payne answers with biblical clarity and practical insight in this follow-up to his classic with Colin Marshall, The Trellis and the Vine . Building on his own exegetical and theological research, Payne unpacks the complementary roles public proclamation and private exhortation play in a healthy local church. In preaching, pastors declare forth God’s Word with conviction, applying Scripture broadly to the whole church. Yet the New Testament also assumes all believers will speak words of wisdom to one another, applying eternal truth to specific life situations. Payne’s point is that if we want to see our churches mature, we must cultivate environments where both kinds of speaking thrive. Every pastor, group leader, and Sunday school teacher will benefit from thoughtful reflection on the ideas Payne presents in Let the Word Dwell Richly . Award of Distinction Timothy St. John, After Church Hurt: Healing in the Care of the Good Shepherd (New Growth) In our therapeutic age, the idea of church hurt is pervasive, and it can feel confusing and even threatening for church leaders. We all—from pastors to members—desperately need a clear understanding of church hurt. And perhaps more, we need a pathway toward preventing it and healing from it. In After Church Hurt , Timothy St. John gives church leaders a gospel-rich and scripturally grounded tool for defining church hurt and navigating through it. Whether you’ve been hurt by the church or are striving to be the kind of leader who does no harm, St. John will help you understand church hurt biblically, learn how to embrace God’s grace, and then move toward church unity without minimizing pain or excusing abuse. This book is highly practical and culturally redemptive. We hope many in the church will read it. Judges: Brandon Cooper, Jared Kennedy, Walt Nilsson, Jen Oshman Christian Living Jen Wilkin, Dust to Dust: Aging Wisely in an Anti-Aging World (Crossway) We’re regularly bombarded with images and messages that tell us our worth is found in how we look and that aging is something to be feared. In Dust to Dust , Jen Wilkin tells us the true story of aging. She helps readers see the stages of life as a chiasm—a mirrored journey that begins and ends with the need for dignity and dependence. In an age where the church is on the cusp of experiencing demographic inversion, we need a stronger theology of aging and a clearer understanding of our Christian duty to love our aging neighbor as ourselves. Wilkin offers biblically robust arguments for seeing and valuing people through the end of life, whether in the context of our biological families or in the broader church family. In this, she pushes against the individualistic, youth-obsessed status quo. Most importantly, Dust to Dust asks readers to ponder their own presuppositions about what makes life meaningful. Spoiler alert: It’s not a fresh-looking face, the absence of gray hair, or the abundance of lean muscle. Wilkin clearly explains that growing in Christlike character and wisdom, even as our bodies decay, is a witness to the watching world of our hope in heaven. Award of Distinction William P. Smith, You Are Not Alone: How God Solves Our Isolation and Loneliness (P&R) In a world of unprecedented connectivity, it seems odd to think of ourselves as alone. Yet nearly everyone in today’s society experiences some level of isolation and loneliness. It’s par for the course in a digital age where we stare at screens instead of faces and live increasingly individualistic lives. In You Are Not Alone , William P. Smith insightfully diagnoses the varying facets of aloneness in modern society, demonstrating that the feeling of being alone isn’t merely about physical separation. Smith identifies and unpacks root issues that cause people to avoid relationships, leave the church, and drift further into a solitary life. Ultimately, Smith presents the overarching gospel story as both the explanation for and the solution to our struggles with isolation and loneliness. When we understand that we’re seen, known, and loved by God, we can move toward community and embrace the relationships we were created for from a deep sense of acceptance i

Dane Ortlund将我们的目光转向辉煌的未来。 凭借神学的深度和一位会向疲惫的灵魂说话的牧师的温柔,他把天堂的希望带到了地上,直接对日常生活的悲伤和斗争说话.
这是一本供基督徒阅读的书, 他们需要提醒人们, 苦难不会是最后一句话, 耶稣会让万事皆新, 你会完成这些渴望回家的页面,
Brett McCracken杰出奖 " 睡眠的智慧:上帝的真理和疲劳的复兴如何安息 " (Zondervan) 如果你今晚能做的最有精神的事情之一 就是闭上眼睛去睡觉呢? 在"睡眠之智慧"中,布雷特·麦克拉肯(Brett McCracken)采取一项活动,我们花了我们生命的大约三分之一时间来做,并揭示出其惊人的神学意义.
他利用圣经、科学和文化洞察力来表明睡眠不是必然的罪恶, 这是来自上帝的礼物;夜以继夜地提醒我们,我们是生物,不是造物主;以及指向我们在基督中永恒安息的路标。
这本书会令你更感激 睡眠的天赋 更惊讶于从未入睡的上帝 法官:约书亚·查特曼、胡安·桑切斯、马特·斯梅特赫斯特、劳拉·斯波丁部长托尼·佩恩、让《言语之井》富足: " 一个又一个言语(Matthias Media)的重要力量 " 福音派人士仍然坚定致力于神语之道。
在我们改革后的传统中,布道——公开宣示言语——恰好在我们礼拜中占据了中心位置。 然而,在我们强调讲解时,我们是否忽略了上帝给予每个基督徒的言语? 我们是否忽视了"新约"作家反复称赞的又一个词?
这些是托尼·佩恩在跟科林·马歇尔(Colin Marshall),"The Trellis"(The Trellis)和"葡萄"(Vine)的经典续作中,以圣经的清晰和切实的见解回答的问题. 佩恩在自己的开天辟地和神学研究的基础上,整理了在健康的地方教会中公开宣布和私下劝告的辅助作用.
在传道中,牧师们坚信地宣布真主的话语,将《圣经》广泛应用于整个教会。 然而"新约"也假定所有信徒都会互相说出智慧的话来,将永恒的真理运用到特定的生活状况. Payne的观点是,如果我们想让我们的教堂成熟,我们必须培育两种语言都兴旺的环境。
每个牧师、团体领袖和星期日的学校老师, Timothy St. John杰出奖,《教堂受创后:在善牧人照料下康复》(新成长) 在我们的治疗时代,教会伤害的想法是普遍存在的,它会感到困惑甚至威胁教会领袖.
我们——从牧师到成员——都迫切需要明确了解教会遭受的伤害。 也许,我们更需要一条路径 来预防它和治愈它。 在"Church Hurt"中,蒂莫西·圣约翰(Timothy St.
圣约翰会帮助你理解教会的伤害, 学习如何接受上帝的恩惠, 然后走向教会团结, 而不减少痛苦或免责。 这本书具有高度实用性和文化上的"红色"发作. 我们希望教会里很多人会读到它.
法官: Brandon Cooper、Jared Kennedy、Walt Nilsson、Jen Oshman Christian Living Jen Wilkin、 " 从尘到尘:在反老龄化世界中明智地老去 " (十字路口) 我们经常被那些告诉我们价值的图像和信息所轰炸, 在"尘至尘"中,仁·威尔金讲述了老化的真实故事.
她帮助读者将人生的各个阶段视为一个奇观——一个以尊严和依赖的需要为起点和终点的镜像之旅。 在教会正面临人口倒置的时代,我们需要一个更强烈的老化神学,需要更清楚地理解我们的基督教义务,爱我们的老邻居,就像我们自己一样。
威尔金为人们通过生命的终结,无论是在我们的生物家庭还是在更广泛的教会家庭中,来看待和重视他们提供了具有圣经意义的有力论据。 在此她推倒了个人主义的,青春主义的现状. 最重要的是,"尘到尘"要求读者思考他们自己的预想是什么让生命有意义.
破坏者警告:这不是一张新相貌,没有灰色发型,或者有丰富的瘦肌肉。 威尔金清楚地解释,在基督般的性格和智慧中成长,即使我们的身体已经衰败,也见证了我们天堂所希望的观察世界. (原始内容存档于2018-10-21). Award of Distriction William P.

威廉·P·史密斯(William P. Smith)在《你并非孤独》中深刻地分析了现代社会中孤独性的不同方面, 史密斯识别并解开导致人们回避关系,离开教堂并更进一步地漂入孤独生活的根源问题.

title: Evening Worship’s Culture-Shaping Power
summary: Don’t wait for the perfect time. Trust the Lord, open the doors, and watch him bless his people.

title_zh: 晚间崇拜的文化塑造力
content: Recently, a friend asked me how things were going at the church where I serve. As I reflected on his question, I was overwhelmed with gratitude. The Lord has been astonishingly kind to our congregation over the past several years. We’ve become healthier, more unified, and more joyful. Then my friend asked a second question: “What changed?” Like many young churches, our early years included growing pains. We loved one another, but not always patiently. We were starting to believe the right truths, but we were still learning to put those truths into action. I thought of several possible answers: faithful elders, growing families, or the cumulative effect of years of expository preaching. Yet as I contemplated, I realized most of the growth in our congregation started with one small decision. Five years ago, our church began gathering at the close of each Lord’s Day for evening worship. Evening worship isn’t a magic formula for church growth or maturity. Christ alone builds his church, but he does use means. I’m convinced that gathering a second time each Lord’s Day has become one of the most significant means by which Christ has shaped the culture of our congregation. Tyranny of the ‘Perfect Time’ When we planted the church in 2013, we began with Sunday school and morning worship. I always hoped we’d eventually add an evening service, but it never seemed to be a good time. Ministry was demanding, other Sunday evening activities filled the calendar, and I worried about whether anyone would even show up. We were waiting for a perfect season that never arrived. None of my reasons for waiting was foolish, but five years later, I can say without hesitation that the Lord has done exceeding, abundantly beyond all we asked or imagined through evening worship. Here are four ways restoring evening worship has shaped our church’s culture. 1. Double Portion of the Means of Grace The most obvious blessing of evening worship is wonderfully simple: It gives our congregation another opportunity each Lord’s Day to gather around the ordinary means of grace. We gather to hear God’s Word read and preached, to pray, to sing his praises, and to enjoy the fellowship of his people. Taken individually, none of these things seems particularly impressive. We’ve become healthier, more unified, and more joyful. When we gather a second time, we aren’t inventing a new program; we’re doubling down on the same apostolic diet that sustained the early church: the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers (Acts 2:42). Those means of grace didn’t expire with the book of Acts; they’re still our Lord’s chosen means for growing his church (v. 47). Often, the conversation about whether to add an evening service begins with the inevitable question: “Does God require evening worship?” While I understand the nature of the question, we’d do better to have the perspective that evening worship isn’t another box to check or a legalistic obligation to bear. It’s an invitation to feast on the grace God delights to give. 2. Sweet, Unhurried Fellowship Evening worship has brought an unexpectedly sweet blessing: It has knitted our church family more tightly together. Sunday evenings have become a space where relationships are genuinely cultivated and deepened. When people gather only on Sunday morning, there’s an understandable urgency. Families often hurriedly arrive just before the prelude and leave soon after the postlude. Conversations are necessarily brief—our members have children to collect, lunches to prepare, and the looming reality of the workweek ahead. Evening worship changes the pace of church life. People tend to arrive earlier and linger longer. Families invite one another over for a meal between services. Friendships that might have taken years to develop in a morning lobby blossom over a casual Sunday evening dinner. Elders have spontaneous shepherding conversations that could never have been scheduled. Over time, we’ve seen these ordinary interactions produce extraordinary fruit. Evening worship has strengthened the communion of the saints, turning the biblical command to “stir up one another to love and good works” from a Sunday morning rush into a Sunday evening reality (Heb. 10:24–25). 3. Reclaiming the Whole Lord’s Day Another blessing of evening worship is the hardest to measure: It has slowly but surely reshaped our weekly habits. By bookending the Sabbath with worship, we’ve seen a cultural transformation in our church from functionally celebrating “the Lord’s Morning” to truly honoring “the Lord’s Day.” Along the way, Sundays have stopped feeling like a brief interruption to our weekend and have become the center around which the rest of our week is ordered. The hours between worship services are no longer time to go our own way before Monday arrives. Instead, the afternoon has become a haven for rest, hospitality, reading, and fellowship. We’re learning what the prophet Isaiah meant when he called the Sabbath a “delight” and the holy day of the Lord “honorable” (Isa. 58:13). I’m particularly excited for the ways this will shape the children of our church for years to come. They’re growing up learning that the Lord’s Day belongs to the Lord, and that worship isn’t something we squeeze into a busy schedule but the reality around which we gladly order our lives. 4. Joy of Costly Worship Gathering on Sunday evening means setting aside other good things—an afternoon of recreation, extra sleep, or the comfort of staying in our pajamas. In a culture that prizes convenience and leisure above all else, making the effort to gather a second time declares to our souls and to our world what we value most. Worship is sacrificial by nature, and therefore it becomes a test for our own hearts to determine if Christ is worthy of our first love. When we offer him only the brief, convenient scraps of our weekend, we flirt with the attitude of ancient Israel, who sniffed at God’s altar and called his worship wearisome (Mal. 1:13). Evening worship offers a corrective. King David understood this principle when he refused to offer burnt offerings to the Lord that “cost [him] nothing” (2 Sam. 24:24). Genuine worship always requires laying aside lesser loves because Christ is worthy of our first love. The cost of evening worship isn’t something churches should apologize for. Every Lord’s Day, our people quietly declare—to our children, to one another, and to our own anxious hearts—that Jesus Christ is worth rearranging our lives for. Members, Don’t Wait If you belong to a church that offers evening worship but you haven’t yet made it a part of your weekly practice, let me encourage you: Start this Sunday. Don’t wait until your schedule clears up or your kids get a little older. Dive into the deep end of the Lord’s Day. You’ll find that the initial sacrifice of your Sunday evening is swallowed up by the unparalleled delight of being with God’s people. Pastors, Don’t Wait Since seeing these blessings, I’ve spoken with many pastors who tell me, “We agree evening worship is good, but this just isn’t the right season for our church.” Genuine worship always requires laying aside lesser loves because Christ is worthy of our first love. I understand that hesitation because I lived it. Ministry is exhausting. We’re already stretched by obligations. But Christ hasn’t promised to build his church through perfect circumstances; he has promised to bless his appointed means. If your church is considering gathering for Lord’s Day evening worship, don’t feel it must be elaborate. Begin simply. Preach the Word. Pray. Sing. Gather God’s people once more before the sun sets, and trust Christ to do what he has always done through ordinary faithfulness. Trust the Lord and Open the Door If I could go back and give my younger, church-planting self one piece of advice, it would be this: Don’t wait for the perfect time. Trust the Lord, open the doors, and watch him bless his people. The fruit will

最近,一个朋友问我,我所在的教堂的情况如何。 我在思考他的问题时感到十分感激。 在过去的几年里,上帝对我们的教友们非常友好 我们变得更健康、更团结、更快乐。
然后,我的朋友问了第二个问题:“什么改变了?” 和许多年轻的教堂一样,我们的早年包括了不断增长的痛苦. 我们彼此相爱,但并不总是耐心的。 我们开始相信正确的真理,但我们仍在学习将这些真理付诸行动。
我想到了几个可能的答案:忠实的长者,不断成长的家庭,或者多年的通俗传道的累积效应. 然而,正如我所想的,我意识到,我们教友会的大部分增长始于一个小决定。 五年前,我们的教堂开始在每逢主节结束时聚集,进行晚间礼拜.
晚上的礼拜不是教会成长或成熟的法术。 基督独自建造他的教堂, 但他确实使用手段。 我深信,每个主日第二次聚会已经成为基督塑造我们教会文化的最重要手段之一。
" 完美时间 " 的暴风雨 2013年植入教堂后,从星期天的学校开始并进行晨祷. 我总是希望我们最终会增加晚间服务, 我担心是否有人会出现。 我们等待着一个从未到来的完美的季节。
我等待的理由都不愚蠢,但是五年后,我可以毫不犹豫地说,上帝已经超越了我们通过晚礼而要求或想象的一切。 以下是四种恢复晚间礼拜的方式, 1. 联合国
双相的恩惠手段 晚上崇拜最明显的祝福是极其简单的: 它使我们的会众再次有机会在每逢主日聚集在普通的恩惠手段周围。 我们聚集一堂,听取上帝的言辞,宣读并宣讲,祈祷,歌颂他,享受他所生人民的友谊.
从个别情况来看,这些事情似乎都不特别令人印象深刻。 我们变得更健康、更团结、更快乐。 当我们第二次聚会时, 我们并没有发明新的计划; 我们正用维持早期教会的同样背信弃义的饮食翻一番:使徒们的教诲、奖学金、断面包和祈祷(第2:42号法案)。
这些恩典并没有随着法令书而过期;它们仍然是我们的主选择的培养他教会的手段(v.47)。
有关是否增加晚间礼拜的谈话往往从一个不可避免的问题开始:“上帝需要晚间礼拜吗?” 虽然我理解问题的性质, 我们最好还是从这个角度来看待晚会礼拜, 以享受上帝赐予的恩惠。 2. 联合国
令人意外地祝福: 它使我们的教会家庭更加紧密地联系在一起。 星期天晚上已成为真正培育和加深关系的空间。 当人们只在星期天早上聚集时,
家人往往在前奏前匆匆赶到,后奏后很快离开. 讨论必然是简短的——我们的成员有孩子要收集,午餐要准备,以及未来工作周即将到来的现实。 晚上的崇拜改变了教会生活的步伐. 人们往往更早到达,更久地停留. 家庭邀请对方 吃饭服务。
友谊可能要花很多年时间 在一个早晨的大厅里发展起来 在一个周日的晚宴上开花 长老们自发地进行牧羊对话,这是永远无法安排的. 随着时间的推移,我们已经看到这些普通的相互作用 产生了非凡的成果。
晚上的崇拜强化了圣徒的圣餐,将圣经的旨意变成了"互相激起,爱与善",从星期天的早晨冲出,变成星期天的晚间现实(Heb. 10:24-25). 3. 庆祝全天主节 晚上礼拜的又一祝福是最难衡量的: 它缓慢但确实改变了我们的每周习惯。
通过将安息日订为崇拜,我们看到了我们教堂的文化转变,从功能上的庆祝"主的早晨"转变为真正地纪念"主的节日". 沿途,周日不再感觉像短暂地中断了我们的周末,成为了我们周余时间订购的中心.
礼拜服务之间的时间 已经没有时间在星期一到来之前走我们自己的路了。 相反,下午已成为休息、招待、阅读和研究金的天堂。 我们正在学习先知以赛亚称安息日为"光明"和主的圣日为"尊贵"(以萨:58:13)的意义.
未来数年, 他们逐渐意识到主日属于主, 礼拜并不是我们忙碌的日程,  4.四.
周日晚会的欢乐, 在一个将方便和休闲放在一切之上的文化中,努力再次聚集起来,向我们的灵魂和世界宣布我们最珍视的东西。
崇拜是天生的牺牲品,因此它成为考验我们自己的心,决定基督是否值得我们初恋. 当我们只向他提供我们周末的短暂、方便的片段时,我们与古代以色列的态度调和,古以色列对上帝的祭坛闻了一闻并称他的崇拜为"疲软"(马勒1:13). 晚上的礼拜提供了一个纠正。
大卫国王之所以理解这一原则,是因为他拒绝向耶和华提供“不使[他]付出任何代价”(2 Sam. 24:24)。 真正的崇拜总是需要放下更少的爱 因为基督值得我们的初恋 晚上礼拜的费用不是教会应该道歉的。
每逢主节,我们的宗族就悄悄地对我们的子孙、彼此和我们自己的心,说:耶稣基督值得我们重新生活。 成员们,不要等待 如果你属于一个提供晚间礼拜的教会,
别等到日程安排结束, 潜入主日深处. 你会发现,你星期天晚上的最初牺牲被与上帝同在的无与伦比的喜悦所吞噬。
牧师们, 别等了, 自从看到这些祝福之后, 我和许多牧师说, “我们同意晚上的礼拜是好事, 真正的崇拜总是需要放下更少的爱 因为基督值得我们的初恋 我理解这种犹豫是因为我活了下来 部正精疲力竭. 我们已不堪重负。
但基督并没有承诺通过完美的环境来建造他的教堂;他已经承诺祝福他指定的手段. 如果你的教堂考虑为主节晚会举行集会, 开始吧 宣说相. 祈祷  Sing唱. 在日出前再次召集上帝的百姓,
相信上帝,打开门 如果我能回去,给我年轻, 教会的自我一个建议, 信从主出,开出门来,看他保佑他的人. 果实会

title: In the Darkness, Christmas Shines a Light
summary: The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves.
summary_zh: 某些花朵 -- -- 日出花朵、罂粟和日出花朵, 空荡荡的街道 安静的房屋被搅动了 我们从休息转向工作,静态转向活动。 我们从休息转向工作,静态转向活动。 我们被太阳能所活化、生长和繁荣。 与神同为也.
title_zh: 在黑暗中，圣诞节照亮光明
content: Read For behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and thick darkness the peoples; but the LORD will arise upon you, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising. (Isa. 60:2–3) Reflect There’s something about a sunrise. It wakes the world. Unlike the jarring blare of an alarm clock, a sunrise quietly whispers “Wake, O sleeper” with the graceful love of a parent rubbing a sleeping child’s back. When the sun rises, the slumbering stir to life. We’ve just spent seven or eight hours dead to the world. Then the sunrise triggers in us what looks like a resurrection. We rise. Certain flowers—daisies, poppies, and the aptly named morning glories—open their blossoms at the sun’s rising. Little by little, empty streets fill and quiet houses stir. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. Drawn to the warmth and energy of the just-unveiled sun, we transition from rest to work, stillness to activity. It’s not surprising that the sun is an oft-used metaphor for God. For he, too, resurrects the dead. He, too, is the Giver of life and growth. He, too, draws all things to himself—such as the trees, which by nature grow upward, toward the sun, their branches like arms raised in perpetual worship. This is the created order. All things were made to be drawn to and sustained by the sun. We were made to be alive insofar as we live, grow, and flourish by solar energy. So too with God. We’re in darkness and death without him. As he bestows his grace on us, we rise to new life. We’re able to grow. Like the sunflower blossom, which turns to follow the sun wherever it’s positioned in the sky, we’re created to look to the Lord, who “will arise upon [us], and his glory will be seen upon [us]” (Isa. 60:2). In a world of darkness, we ache for the light. We wait for the sunrise. All nations, all kings, all people share this in common. The horizon each of us looks to—the nature of the “new day” we await—may be different: A new job. A remodeled home. A regime change. But only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. His is “the true light, which gives light to everyone” (John 1:9). Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled in him. Only the sunrise of Christ will eternally satisfy. The general revelation of God’s created order—darkness and light, night and day—primes every created thing to know they need light, a salvation from outside themselves. The special revelation of Christ reveals a truer light than even the sun: the light that is our eternal life, the light the darkness will never overcome (v. 5), the light that will one day end night as we know it (Rev. 22:5). Respond How is God’s glory seen in your life? How are you reflecting his beauty? In contrast to those who dwell in darkness, how does your life reflect 1 Thessalonians 5:5: “You are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness”?

title: Editor’s Pick: Middle-Grade Books
summary: The best children’s literature does more than preach to us; it draws us into the story while pointing toward truth, goodness, and beauty.
summary_zh: 我还在读儿童书籍。 有时我会重读我小时候所欣赏的同一本书:纳尼亚纪事、伯特·布林的"巴恩"、"小不列颠"、"侦探"弗雷迪和"哈地男孩"。 有时,我读到一些新书 出来吸引我的注意力, 如"游牧地的老师" 或最新的绿色Ember系列。 我读我以前最爱的作品的经验 与成年人不同 我仍然喜欢那些更古老的故事,但我有时会想知道弗兰克和乔·哈迪在经历了这么多脑震荡之后的后些年表现如何.
title_zh: 编辑精选：中年级读物
content: I still read children’s books. Sometimes I reread the same books I enjoyed as a child: The Chronicles of Narnia , Bert Breen’s Barn , Little Britches , Freddy the Detective , and The Hardy Boys . Sometimes I read newer books that come out that catch my attention, like The Teacher of Nomad Land or the latest in the Green Ember series. My experience of reading my old favorites is different as an adult. I still enjoy the older stories, but I sometimes wonder how Frank and Joe Hardy fared in their later years after getting so many concussions. I often enjoy the new stories, though I’m certain I don’t experience them the same way the target audience does, which is a little like knowing Narnia exists and not getting to visit it again for a long time. In his book Make Believe: On Telling Stories to Children , Mac Barnett explains what makes for a good children’s novel: “The best children’s writers tell the truth in a way that is recognizable and authentic to children.” The key is truth and connection with the audience. C. S. Lewis said something similar in his essay “ On Three Ways of Writing for Children ” many years ago. Children’s books helped me process the world. I read a lot of junk as a child, but I read a lot of good books too. And the good books were the ones that helped me understand why I was feeling frustration over a teacher’s unfairness, resentment about a classmate’s teasing, or fear of the turmoil in the adult world that streamed at me through the radio and television. The best sorts of children’s literature teach us something. Barnett caused a kerfuffle when his little book came out because he declared that “94.7 percent of kids’ books are crud.” He had in his sights overtly didactic books, with the industrial complex of volumes telling kids to “be kind” ad nauseam in his crosshairs. Quality children’s literature does more than preach to us; it draws us into the story while pointing toward truth, goodness, and beauty. I’ve put together a list of middle-grade books (though Barnett dislikes that label) that have been published in the last year or so. I enjoyed them because they told a story well and I learned something about the truth along the way. 1. Jonathan Rogers, The Charlatan’s Boy (Rabbit Room Press, 2026) Most children’s literature is, in some sense, about identity. That’s a major theme in The Charlatan’s Boy , as Grady travels around Corenwald with Floyd, the man who found him as a baby. When townspeople stop believing in feechiefolk—the mysterious residents of Feechiefen Swamp—Grady can no longer make a living by pretending to be a feechie. Instead, Floyd puts him on display as the ugliest boy alive. Though I suspected where the story would end, I didn’t want to put the book down because I couldn’t tell what Grady and Floyd were going to do next. It’s simply a well-told story. But I also appreciated that the whole story subtly reminds readers that durable identity is received, not chosen. It’s the best sort of book that captures the imagination even as it points us toward truth. 2. S. D. Smith, The Lost Cause (Story Warren, 2026) The publication of a new Green Ember book was cause for celebration when my kids were younger. The saying “It will not be so in the Mended Wood” became part of our household vernacular shortly after we met Picket, Heather, and Helmer for the first time. And although my children are past the age where it’s cool to be interested in rabbits with swords, my publicity copies of Smith’s books mysteriously disappear from my to-be-read stack before I get to them. I love these stories because they make me long for goodness, truth, and beauty. In a culture of sarcasm and skepticism, Smith reminds us that virtues like hope, loyalty, and perseverance are worth striving for. The Lost Cause is the third book in a sequence within the world of Natalia. It’s not the best place to jump into the story; those new to the series would be well served by beginning with The Green Ember , or at least the first in this sequence, The Lost Key . If you’re building a home library for your middle-grade readers, the Green Ember series is a great place to start. 3. Ben Palpant, Brightwing Tales: Acorn’s Misadventure (Brightwing Books, 2026) I came across Palpant’s work with his nonfiction book, An Axe for the Frozen Sea , a series of interviews with Christian poets about beauty, wonder, and art. His Brightwing Tales are the sort of children’s stories you’d expect from someone who loves good poetry. The first volume in the series, Brightwing Tales: Mole’s Misadventure , weaves a narrative about Mr. Mole through episodic chapters. It includes ghost stories, a hungry cat, a quest for pie, and a beautiful love story. Some of the scenes Palpant describes are so poignantly beautiful they brought tears to my eyes. The world reminded me of Wind in the Willows and Winnie-the-Pooh even before I read the description on his website. This second volume, Brightwing Tales: Acorn’s Misadventure , has a stronger narrative arc as it recounts the unusual friendship between a mouse named Acorn and Bear (who is a bear). It’s a story of loss, of longing, and of redemption. This is the sort of book that can shape a child’s imagination, helping him or her to see the goodness of the world even when everything looks dark. I enjoyed reading it myself and look forward to reading it to grandchildren one day. 4. Kathryn Butler, Escape from Rome (Crossway, 2026) I read dozens of Choose Your Own Adventure stories as a kid. Many of them on the school bus. Those books let me find treasure, die at the hands of pirates, get lost in outer space, and rescue damsels in distress all in one afternoon. They were a long way from highbrow literature, but the series was fun. Butler has two Decide-as-You-Go Adventures in Crossway’s Lamplight series, which use a similar format. In Escape from Rome , a summer visit to a cousin ends up with a broken lamp, a time-traveling adventure, and choices that have consequences. Will you admit to breaking the lamp or try to shift the blame? Will you get stuck in ancient Rome or will you make it back to the present? Every decision leads down a different path, sometimes to unpredictable results. Part of the fun is trying to navigate through all the possible pathways. I enjoyed this book as a bit of nostalgia, but I know one young reader at church who absolutely loves the books for their own sakes. 5. Paul Cox, Martin Williams, and Joy Williams, John Calvin’s Illustrated Institutes: The Word of God (P&R, 2026) One of my concerns as a parent and a pastor is that we’re not effective at communicating the basis for our beliefs to the next generation. We need more theology. That doesn’t necessarily mean we need our kids reading thousand-page systematic theologies and listening to formal lectures. We need to put the cookies on the bottom shelf. That’s what the graphic novel adaptation of John Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion does; it presents the core of Calvin’s doctrinal teaching in a visually engaging and intellectually stimulating format. I’ve generally been skeptical of graphic novels, but then I thought about how much I learned about philosophy from poring over Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes as a kid. This illustrated adaption of the Institutes can help introduce the next generation to the basics of Reformed theology. The series is a delightful reminder that theology is for everyone. 6. John Bunyan, adapted by Tyler Van Halteren, Christian’s Quest (Lithos Kids, 2026) There are many adaptations of Bunyan’s classic, The Pilgrim’s Progress . There’s good reason for that, since it’s been one of the best-selling Christian books in history. Important themes about the Christian life are illustrated well and are part of the Christian imaginary, but Bunyan’s archaic language makes it especially hard for young people to read. Van Halteren’s adapted prose, with Manuel Zepic’s illustrations, maintains the spirit of the original while making it

我读我以前最爱的作品的经验 与成年人不同 我仍然喜欢那些更古老的故事,但我有时会想知道弗兰克和乔·哈迪在经历了这么多脑震荡之后的后些年表现如何.

Mac Barnett在其著作《让儿童相信:向儿童讲述故事》中,解释了什么是好儿童小说:“最好的儿童作家以儿童能识别和真实的方式讲述真相。 ” 关键在于真相和与观众的联系. C.S.Lewis在多年前的论文《为儿童写作的三种方式》中也说过类似的话。
儿童书籍帮助我处理世界。 我小时候读了很多垃圾 但我也读了很多好书 优秀的书籍帮助我理解为什么我对老师的不公平感、对同学取笑的怨恨,或者对通过广播和电视向我流传的成人世界的动荡感到沮丧。
最好的儿童文学告诉我们一些东西。 巴内特在小书发表时引发了一场骚动,因为他宣称“94.7%的孩子的书被砸了。 ” 在他眼中,他有公开的教学书籍,其中的工业类的卷子告诉孩子们在他的交叉发作中“友善”地作呕。 高质量的儿童文学对我们来说不仅仅是传道;

该系列的第一卷"闪亮的故事:莫尔的意外"(Brightwing Tales: Mole's Misadventure),通过零星的章节来编织关于莫尔先生的叙事. 它包括了鬼故事,一只饥饿的猫,对派的追求,以及美丽的爱情故事. Palpant描述的一些场景非常美丽,它们给我带来眼泪.
